title: Unstable AF: synchronised cardioversion
stem: Resus 2. A 65-year-old woman has had palpitations, chest tightness and breathlessness for 2 hours. HR 160 irregular, BP 80/50, RR 26, SpO2 93%, GCS 15 but sweaty and frightened. An IV cannula is in. Manage her tachyarrhythmia.
notes:
Checked against Resuscitation Council UK 2025 (tachycardia algorithm; 2021 algorithm unchanged in principle), ESC 2024 AF guidelines and AHA 2025 ACLS.

Adverse features (RCUK): shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, severe heart failure. Any of these in a tachyarrhythmia → synchronised DC cardioversion, up to 3 attempts, under sedation or anaesthesia by someone skilled; then amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 minutes and repeat the shock; then 900 mg over 24 hours.

Energy for AF: your notes use AHA 2025 (200 J biphasic for AF and flutter, 100 J for narrow regular and monomorphic VT; escalate). ERC/RCUK suggest a high initial energy for AF (at or near maximum, commonly 150–200 J), and 70–120 J for regular narrow complex tachycardia and flutter. The station accepts a high initial energy for AF and scores sync mode, safety and re-sync.

Haemodynamic instability overrides the usual 48-hour anticoagulation rule: give heparin at the time of cardioversion if it does not delay it. Never shock unsynchronised for AF: a shock on the T wave can cause VF. Adenosine has no role in AF. Rate-control calcium channel blockers or beta-blockers are dangerous in hypotension.

steps.label: Assess
steps.hint: ABCDE and the adverse features; a 12-lead if it doesn't delay.

ABCDE.r: HR 160 irregularly irregular, BP 80/50, cool peripheries, CRT 4 s.
Tight central chest pain since it started.

ECG.r: Irregularly irregular narrow complex tachycardia, no P waves, rate about 160: AF with fast ventricular response. Rate-related ST depression.
ECG.mark: Interprets AF with fast ventricular response

steps.label: Decide
steps.hint: Adverse features present: synchronised DC cardioversion now.

opts.t: Unstable AF — shock and ischaemia: synchronised DC cardioversion now
opts.mark: Recognises adverse features and chooses DC cardioversion

opts.r: Adenosine does not terminate AF; it can transiently slow the rate only.
Calcium channel blockers in hypotension can cause collapse (and are dangerous if pre-excited).

opts.t: Hold off: she's been in AF for 2 hours, check for clot with an echo first
opts.r: Instability overrides the anticoagulation delay. Shock now; heparin with it.

steps.label: Cardiovert
steps.hint: Consent, sedation with airway kit, pads, SYNC on and seen on the R waves, high energy for AF, all clear, re-check.

opts.t: Anaesthetist or skilled sedationist; airway kit and suction; oxygen
opts.mark: Sedation by a skilled operator with airway kit

opts.t: Press SYNC; check a marker sits on each R wave
opts.mark: Synchronised mode confirmed on the R waves

opts.t: Select a high energy for AF (e.g. 200 J biphasic)
Sedate (e.g. small doses of propofol or ketamine)
Charge, 'all clear, oxygen away', hold the shock button until it fires
opts.mark: Safe delivery: all clear, hold until discharge
opts.r: A short pause, then the shock fires on the R wave. Sinus rhythm at 84.

opts.t: Check rhythm and pulse; re-select SYNC before any further shock

opts.r: A shock on the T wave can cause VF.

steps.label: After
steps.hint: ABCDE, 12-lead, bloods including K and Mg, anticoagulation, cause, admit.

opts.mark: Looks for causes: electrolytes, thyroid, ischaemia

opts.t: Heparin now; long-term anticoagulation by CHA2DS2-VA
If it had failed three times: amiodarone 300 mg over 10–20 min, then shock again
opts.mark: Knows the escalation after 3 failed shocks

qs.a: Shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure
wrong: Rate over 100 with palpitations and anxiety
Fever, rash, vomiting and abdominal pain

qs.q: Why must the shock be synchronised?
qs.a: To avoid a shock on the T wave (R-on-T VF)
wrong: It uses less energy per shock
It is less painful than an unsynchronised shock
It only works if the patient is in sinus rhythm

qs.a: Amiodarone 300 mg over 10–20 min, then shock
wrong: Adenosine 12 mg, then a fourth synchronised shock
Switch to an unsynchronised 360 J shock
Stop, rate-control, and observe on the ward

qs.q: When is an unsynchronised shock appropriate?
wrong: Fast AF with a rate over 180

qs.q: AF for 2 hours with shock — do you wait for anticoagulation?
qs.a: No: give heparin and cardiovert now
wrong: Yes, a TOE must exclude clot first
Only if the CHA2DS2-VA score is zero

badge.name: In Sync
badge.flavor: Adverse features mean electricity. SYNC on, markers on the R waves.

options: Oral beta-blocker and review in clinic

cards.q: AHA 2025 initial synchronised energy for AF?
cards.note: ERC/RCUK: high initial energy for AF.

cards.q: Initial energy for regular narrow complex SVT (AHA)?
Amiodarone loading dose in unstable tachycardia after failed shocks?
options: 150 mg as a rapid bolus push

cards.q: Why is adenosine not useful in AF?
options: The AV node is not part of the AF circuit
It is only licensed for ventricular tachycardia
It precipitates VF in most patients with AF
Its half-life is too long for a fast rhythm
cards.why: It may transiently slow the ventricular rate but will not convert AF.

cards.q: Before each repeat synchronised shock you must…
cards.why: Many devices default to unsynchronised after a shock.
